title: What the Law Could Not Do
english: …the blessed David: “I said in my alarm, ‘Every man is a liar’” (Psalm 116:11). The same reasoning would apply to God and to us in all other matters too; for example, in the matter of righteousness. For one could say, and not unreasonably, “Let God be righteous, and every man unrighteous.”

“But if our unrighteousness shows the righteousness of God” (Romans 3:5). The occasion for this slander arose in this way. After the return from Babylon, the sons of Israel, ordered by Cyrus to rebuild the temple, to pay their vows and to offer sacrifices, grew slack, pleading poverty and the hardship left by the captivity. For this they were corrected by measured chastisements: failed harvests and lack of rain (Haggai 1:9–11). Chafing at such blows, they called the foreigners and those who did not serve God happy, as living in good cheer, and said that those people were better off than they were. And so the prophet Malachi said to them: “You have made your words heavy against me, says the Lord. And you said, ‘How have we spoken against you?’ You said,” he says, “‘It is vain to serve God. What more have we gained because we kept his charges, and because we walked as suppliants before the Lord Almighty? And now we call strangers happy, and those who do lawless deeds are built up; they opposed God and were saved.’ This is how those who feared the Lord spoke against him, each to his neighbor; and the Lord gave heed and heard” (Malachi 3:13–16).

For this reason, he says, some thought that the Jews were saying, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Romans 3:8). But when he says that their condemnation is just, he means those who pinned those words on the Jews, or rather those who dared to say, “Let us do evil so that good may come.”

“But now the righteousness of God has been made manifest apart from the law” (Romans 3:21). I know that it is written of certain people that “they were both righteous, walking blameless in the commandments and ordinances of Christ” (Luke 1:6); and the blessed Paul too said that he himself had become “blameless as to the righteousness that is in the law” (Philippians 3:6). But one who is blameless in these things has not yet done the deeds that will make him illustrious and renowned. Indeed, the blessed Paul himself said again that he counted everything in the law as loss and reckoned it as so much refuse, and that he would seek instead “the surpassing excellence of the knowledge of Christ” (Philippians 3:7–8).

Again, the law condemns those who transgress; that is why he says elsewhere, “For if there was glory in the ministry of condemnation, much more does the ministry of righteousness abound in glory” (2 Corinthians 3:9). And since the law contains a great many commandments, even the careful keeper of the law must surely stumble in some of them and become a transgressor of the law. The inspired disciples plainly admitted that it is truly burdensome, for they said: “Now therefore, why are you putting God to the test by placing on the neck of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

title: Justified Freely in Christ
english: When, then, the Greeks were under sin for not knowing the Creator, and the Jews as guilty of transgressing the law, those on the earth necessarily had need of Christ, who justifies. For we have been justified “not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his great mercy” (Titus 3:5). For it was he who long ago said through the voice of the prophets, “I am he who blots out your transgressions, and I will not remember them” (Isaiah 43:25). Justifying grace passes to all alike, I mean to Jews and Greeks, because “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23). The glory of God may fittingly be understood as this: neither to know how to do wrong nor to be of a nature that can do wrong. And the whole created order surely falls short of the glories of the Godhead, for even some of the angels slipped. Yet God the Father was pleased “to sum up all things in Christ” (Ephesians 1:10), who justifies freely by his grace (Romans 3:24). For he has been set forth as a propitiation through faith in his blood (Romans 3:25). Since he made his own blood the price given in exchange for the life of all, he has saved the world under heaven and made the Father and God in heaven merciful and kindly toward us.

“Where then is boasting? It is excluded” (Romans 3:27). For who at all will boast, or in what, when all have become worthless and turned aside from the straight way, and there is no one at all who does good (Psalm 14:3; Romans 3:12)? So, he says, boasting is excluded; that is, it has been thrown out and done away with, and has no place at all among us. And how was it excluded? We have been enriched with the forgiveness of sins committed before (Romans 3:25), being justified freely, by mercy and grace, in Christ.

“Do we then nullify the law through faith?” (Romans 3:31). The God of all said to the inspired Moses: “I will raise up for them a prophet like you from among their brothers, and I will put my word in his mouth, and he will speak to them whatever I command him. And the man who does not listen to his words, whatever the prophet speaks in my name, I will take vengeance on him” (Deuteronomy 18:18–19). How then do we not uphold the law through faith, when we receive the word that comes from him? Emmanuel has been called a prophet because of his humanity, standing, as it were, in the place of Moses as mediator between God and men (1 Timothy 2:5). And again, the law was in shadows, yet it is seen to be in labor with the form of the truth; and the truth does not abolish the types but makes them clearer.

“For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God” (Romans 4:2). I think, someone has said, that those who look closely into the account of our forefather Abraham ought to say this: it has been said somewhere by one of the holy disciples that faith without works is dead (James 2:26). title: Abraham's Faith and the Father's Love
english: …altar?” (James 2:21). Do the Spirit-bearing writers, then, say things contrary to one another? What, then, do we say to this? To him, when he was already far on in years, the God of all promised a son, quite beyond all expectation, and said that the offspring to come from him would rival the countless multitude of the stars (Genesis 15:5). And because he honored the one who promised, bearing witness to God by this that he can accomplish all things, he was justified before him (Genesis 15:6), and received, as a reward worthy of so God-loving a mind, the forgetting of his former offences. In due course God made the oracle concerning Isaac a trial for the righteous man (Genesis 22:1–2); but in this too he was faithful and loved God, as one who put nothing ahead of his love for God. Yet, as the Savior's disciple says, “Faith was working together with the works, and by the works faith was made firm” (James 2:22). And the admirable Paul himself said somewhere of our forefather Abraham: “By faith he offered up Isaac when he was tested; he who had received the promises was offering up his only son, he to whom it was said, ‘Through Isaac shall your offspring be named’; for he reasoned that God is able even to raise from the dead” (Hebrews 11:17–19). So even if it should perhaps be said that he was justified by works because, when tested, he offered up Isaac, this too was for him a clear proof of the firmest faith.

“Not only that, but we also boast in God” (Romans 5:11). Our Lord Jesus Christ, making plain the truly admirable love of God the Father which he showed toward us, brought forward as proof the goal of his work in the flesh and his suffering on the cross, saying somewhere: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16). For he truly gave his own Son for us; and we have been redeemed, set free from death and sin. For the Word “became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14) for no other reason than this: that by enduring the death of the flesh he might triumph over the rulers and authorities (Colossians 2:15) and destroy “the one who has the power of death, that is,” Satan (Hebrews 2:14); that he might do away with corruption and, with it, remove the sin that had tyrannized over us; and that he might thus make powerless from then on that ancient curse which human nature underwent in Adam, as in the firstfruits of the race and as in its first root. For Adam, by transgressing the commandment, offended his Creator; that is why he became both accursed and subject to death. But the Master of all took pity again on those who were utterly lost. For the Son came down from heaven, forgiving offences, justifying the ungodly by faith (Romans 4:5), and, as God, reforging human nature into incorruption and bringing it back to what it was in the beginning.
